title_r: The influence of masculinity threat on men's rape myth acceptance
abstract_r: Sexual violence is a global health issue that affects millions of men and women worldwide (World Health Organization, 2013). Using data from 2000 until 2018, the World Health Organization (WHO; 2021) estimated that the lifetime prevalence of physical and sexual intimate partner violence experienced by women over the age of 15 was 26%, 95% CI [22%, 30%]. Using the same data, they also estimated that 6% of women, 95% CI [2%, 6%], experienced non-intimate partner sexual violence at least once in their lives. Researchers have identified a multitude of sociocultural factors that facilitate sexual violence (e.g., Johnson & Johnson, 2021). One of the psychological factors contributing to the prevalence of sexual violence is the acceptance of so-called rape myths. Rape myths are commonly held false beliefs regarding rape, its perpetrators, and its victims (Burt, 1980; Lonsway & Fitzgerald, 1994). The acceptance of rape myths is typically measured by agreement to statements such as “interpreting harmless gestures as “sexual harassment” is a popular weapon in the battle of the sexes” (Gerger et al., 2007). This acceptance has been found to predict the perpetration of acts of sexual violence (Fansher & Zedaker, 2022; Trottier et al., 2021; Yapp & Quayle, 2018). Men are more likely to be perpetrators of sexual violence than women (e.g., Bundeskriminalamt, 2023; Jeffrey & Senn, 2025) and are less likely to be victims, albeit a substantial share of men also suffer from sexual violence and/or coercion (Weiss, 2010). They typically also show a much higher acceptance of rape myths than women (e.g., Davies et al., 2012). This begs the question as to why men perpetrate sexual violence at a much higher rate than women do. While finding the answer to this question is an interdisciplinary effort, the field of social psychology offers a yet perhaps overlooked explanation. Past research in social psychology has shown that perceived challenges to their gender identity lead men to behave more aggressively (Bosson, 2025; Bosson et al., 2009; Braly et al., 2017), perform riskier actions (Vandello et al., 2008; Weaver et al., 2013), and to show more negative attitudes towards minorities (Glick et al., 2007; Talley & Bettencourt, 2008). Researchers have proposed a precarious manhood theory (PMT; Vandello et al., 2008; Vandello & Bosson, 2013) which argues that threat to a man’s gender identity facilitates compensatory behaviors such as aggression and risk-taking in an attempt to restore the threatened identity. An important moderator of this relationship is the extent to which people belief that manhood is a fleeting state, leading to the development of the Precarious Manhood Beliefs (PMB) Scale (Vandello et al., 2008). Several studies have indicated that PMB play an important role in understanding interindividual differences in the reaction to masculinity threats (Himmelstein et al., 2019; O’Connor et al., 2017). One way to compensate for a masculinity threat might be the acceptance of rape myths. An earlier study found that when presented with descriptions of date rape and sexual coercion scenarios, gender-threatened men reacted by putting more blame on the victim and less responsibility on the perpetrator (Munsch & Willer, 2012). In a more recent experiment comparing men only, Vescio et al. (2025) showed that men subjected to gender-incongruent and threatening feedback had a higher acceptance of rape myths than non-threatened men. The gender knowledge test the researchers adapted from Rudmann & Fairchild (2004) is a widely used experimental manipulation in masculinity threat research. One disadvantage of the test is that some items are specific to the US context (e.g., questions about the legal framework for hunting), while others are specific to western culture in general. The present study builds on this work by directly assessing attitude changes in both men and women as measured by a rape myth scale (Gerger et al., 2007) following an experimental manipulation of masculinity threat. In doing so, we aim to replicate the masculinity threat effect on rape myth acceptance using a culturally invariant experimental manipulation of masculinity threat (Sinclair & Carlsson, 2013; Weaver et al., 2013), while investigating PMB as a potential moderator.

title_r: Vis Repligogy: Towards a Culture of Facilitating Replication Studies in Visualization Pedagogy and Research
abstract_r: In this paper, we present the Vis Repligogy framework that enables conducting replication studies in the class. Replication studies are crucial to strengthening the data visualization field and ensuring its foundations are solid and methods accurate. Although visualization researchers acknowledge the epistemological significance of replications and their necessity to establish trust and reliability, the field has made little progress to support the publication of such studies and, importantly, provide methods to the community to encourage replications. Therefore, we contribute Vis Repligogy, a novel framework to systematically incorporate replications within visualization course curricula that not only teaches students replication and evaluation methodologies but also results in executed replication studies to validate prior work. To validate the feasibility of the framework, we present case studies of two graduate data visualization courses that implemented it. These courses resulted in a total of five replication studies. Finally, we reflect on our experience implementing the Vis Repligogy framework to provide useful recommendations for future use. We envision this framework will encourage instructors to conduct replications in their courses, help facilitate more replications in visualization pedagogy and in research, and support a culture shift towards reproducible research. Supplemental materials of this paper are available at https://osf.io/ncb6d/.

abstract_r: The existence of transfer effects of video games on cognitive performance are controversially discussed in experimental psychology. The design of the conceptual replication was based on a comprehensive compilation of the methods used by previous literature on this topic and advanced in order to reach a high scientific state-of-the-art standard. title_r: Sequential dynamics of prediction : from shifting to biasing of decision thresholds
abstract_r:
Assuming the fundamental and pervasive cognitive operation of prediction—even about objectively unpredictable events—the role of prediction in a trial-by-trial sequential effect on choice speed was studied: the adverse between-choice (ABC) sequential effect. As identified in lexical decision, this effect involves faster responses on word and nonword trials after a word trial. This effect is distinct to more generally observed sequential effectsthat, in terms of the parameters of evidence-accumulation models (EAMs) of choice performance, can be explained by biasing thresholds to local choice probability. In contrast, the ABC effect can be explained by prospective threshold shifting: Rather than biasing thresholds, the total evidence required across choices(response caution) is shifted up or down according to the choice made on the previous trial. Lower response caution after a word trial thereby leads to faster word and nonword responses on the next trial. Alternatively, the ABC effect can be explained by sequential variations in accumulation rates, with the rates becoming positively or negatively correlated between trials depending on prior stimulus difficulty. The relative roles of these mechanisms in producing the ABC effect remained to be empirically determined, while the effect potentially offered insight into how prediction dynamically influences serial decisions—by prospective threshold shifts, not only by threshold biasing.
A review of studies reporting the ABC effect identified two common procedural constraints in earlier studies: short time-on-task and long response-stimulus interval (RSI). Explaining the ABC effect by threshold shifting under these conditions implicated the relation between response caution and speed/accuracy trade-off (SATO)—that the effect is a by-product of strategic learning of a SATO policy in early trials that is contingent on the temporal opportunity to volitionally shift thresholds between trials. Explaining the ABC effect by autocorrelation of accumulation rates, in contrast, should be favoured by short RSI without being constrained by time-on-task, and without such strategic implications. Replicating the effect, manipulating these conditions, and comparing EAMs of the data, were undertaken to test these hypotheses and examine these implications.
In replication attempts using data from Mega Lexicon Projects (MLPs), the ABC effect was only observed in those MLPs with RSIs of at least 1700 ms, and relatively few pre-formal practice trials, and then only within their first 500 formal trials. Fitting the data to EAMs of lexical decision, model comparison favoured a choice-dynamic model with one-back target effects on threshold shifting and biasing, and on non-decision time, with the shifting effect constrained by RSI and time-on-task in the same way as seen for response time. This supported the explanation of the ABC effect by early threshold shifting, with a likely role in strategic development of SATO policy. Furthermore, in later trials (up to 20,000), threshold biasing with a cost-benefit pattern on choice speed became dominant, although both shifting and biasing occurred for initial word trials, suggesting parallel development of SATO policy and cost-benefit prediction. Reinforcement learning models further revealed that threshold biasing was informed by choice (base) probabilities rather than repetition probabilities, further implicating their production by response rather than stimulus processes.
A prospective study of the effects of time-on-task and RSI on threshold shifting was then made in a new experiment. The role of speed/accuracy-stress—which was variously constrained in the MLPs— was also examined, as was the difficulty of word and nonword decisions (per word frequency, and nonword base frequency). Uniformity of target and transition sequencing was controlled to account for an issue of target non-randomness that could be statistically identified within a subset of the MLPs and that could qualify interpretation of their sequential effects. The experiment involved 88 participants run through 6 × 160-trial blocks of a web-based lexical decision task, with three consecutive blocks per the within-subject speed- and accuracy-stress manipulation, and with between-subject RSIs of 1s and 2s. Results showed pervasive repetition effects for both choices— except for an ABC effect in the first block under the long 2s RSI, and only substantially under accuracy stress. This confirmed that the ABC effect depends on the temporal opportunity for volitional threshold control, in relatively unpracticed trials.
A further experiment examined what it is about the one-back trial that cues threshold shifting. The review, archival analyses, and the former experiment all pointed to a limited role of within-choice difficulty, and so of shifting per one-back ease of evaluation. A response-based explanation was, alternatively, rationalised, assuming a role for task-wide response and error-management biases between words and nonwords. The issue was tested by changing the lexical decision task by instruction into one of error detection where nonwords were assigned the “yes” response. It was hypothesised that this could flip the sign of the ABC effect between choices—so that caution is downshifted after a nonword response. This was tested in a web-based experiment involving three 160-trial blocks administered to 22 participants. Even as nonword responses remained slower than word responses, the ABC effect was no longer evident except that, within the per-participant scatter of effects across 40-trial sub-blocks, the early operation of a nonword repetition effect was detected in the presence of a small word alternation effect. A response-related, strategic basis to the ABC effect was therefore indicated in its sensitivity to task instruction independently of stimulus difficulty.
In summary, this research identified how prospective changes in decision thresholds produce sequential effects on performance in lexical decision. These effects were firstly dominated by dynamic shifts of overall decision thresholds based on the previous choice in a way that supports learning to optimize SATO. The initial ABC effect that resulted from threshold shifting quickly gave way to threshold biases according to local choice probability as a cost-benefit pattern involving higher-order sequences came to dominate performance. The change with time-on-task in the form of sequential effects can thereby signify the evolution of SATO policy, and a transition from more controlled prediction of overall evidence requirements to more automatic prediction of relative evidence requirements. These observations are likely to generalise to any task that, like lexical decision, involves a between-choice response bias and difference in evaluative difficulty.

title_r: Identification of novel breast cancer susceptibility loci in meta-analyses conducted among Asian and European descendants
abstract_r: Known risk variants explain only a small proportion of breast cancer heritability, particularly in Asian women. To search for additional genetic susceptibility loci for breast cancer, here we perform a meta-analysis of data from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) conducted in Asians (24,206 cases and 24,775 controls) and European descendants (122,977 cases and 105,974 controls). We identified 31 potential novel loci with the lead variant showing an association with breast cancer risk at P < 5 × 10-8. The associations for 10 of these loci were replicated in an independent sample of 16,787 cases and 16,680 controls of Asian women (P < 0.05). In addition, we replicated the associations for 78 of the 166 known risk variants at P < 0.05 in Asians. These findings improve our understanding of breast cancer genetics and etiology and extend previous findings from studies of European descendants to Asian women.

summary: Working Together Online Experiment Preregistration – multi-wave data collection

Data Collection: We will recruit N = 825 participants from MTurk and randomly assign them to one of two task conditions: working together or working individually. In both cases, participants will complete the Lost at Sea task and will have up to 15 minutes to complete the task (Nemiroff & Pasmore, 2001).  We will limit our recruitment to only those participants who have completed at least a 4-year college degree to control for experience with problem-solving tasks and isolate the effect of social class background on task performance. We will also limit recruitment to those ≤35 years of age to increase the relevance of social class background to participants’ experiences. To be able to collect a large enough sample given our recruitment criteria (BA+ and ≤35 years of age), we will collect data in 3 separate waves of N = 275. We will not analyze the data prior to collection of the full sample of N = 825.

Power Analysis: We determined our sample size by conducting an a priori power analysis based on the effect size obtained in similar previous studies (f = 0.11). The power analysis indicated that we would need a final sample size of N = 708 to reliably detect our effects at 80% power. 

We anticipate that we will need to exclude roughly N = 100 participants – to account for both those who fail embedded attention check items, and those who are assigned to the working together condition but are not successfully matched with a partner (a byproduct of the Chatplat software that we will utilize to pair participants together in the working together condition; cf. Wood-Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011). We should be left with a final sample large enough to detect our effects if we recruit approximately 825 total participants.

Hypotheses: Our goal is to test the following two hypotheses:

1)	Task Performance
a.	Participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will perform worse than participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working individually condition.
b.	In contrast, groups of participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will perform better than groups of participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working together condition.

2)	Subjective Task Experience
a.	Participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will have a worse experience than participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working individually condition.
b.	In contrast, participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will have a better experience than participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working together condition.

3)	Groups of participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will report more positive experience of working together (e.g., more integrativeness and coordination) than groups of participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working together condition.

4)	Experience of working together (e.g., e.g., more integrativeness and coordination) will mediate the relationship between social class and task performance.

•	IV: Participants’ social class background (WK vs. MD)

WK = both parents’ highest education level < 4-year college degree vs.
MD = at least one parent’s highest education level ≥ 4-year college degree

•	IV: Task Condition (individually vs. together)
◦	Working individually: participants will complete the Lost at Sea task individually
◦	Working together: participants will complete the Lost at Sea task with a partner via a Chatplat chat, they will be put in social-class-matched pairs based on their 

•	DV: Task Performance 
◦	Yoked deviation score – will average across two similar individuals to be able to compare performance across working individually vs. together conditions

•	DV: Subjective Experience with Task
◦	Mean of 5 items: how comfortable, how natural, how well, to what extent did you perform up to your potential, how well do you think you did relative to other participants 

•	Working Together Mediator: Experience of working together (will take average of two partner scores)
◦	How much did you and your partner integrate each other's ideas?  
◦	To what extent did you and your partner share information with each other?
◦	How comfortable was it for you and your partner to work together?
◦	How natural was it for you and your partner to work together?
◦	To what extent did you and your partner cooperate to get the work done?
◦	How positively did you and your partner respond to each other? 
◦	How much did you and your partner affirm each other's ideas? 

•	Covariate: Carefulness
◦	How careful were you when completing the task? 
◦	How seriously did you take the task?

•	Covariate: Familiarity 
◦	How familiar are you with task? 

Analysis Plan

•	We will conduct the following analyses of direct effects:
◦	Social Class X Task Condition --> Task Performance
◦	Social Class X Task Condition --> Task Performance
◦	Social Class X Task Condition --> Subjective Task Experience
◦	(Working Together condition only): Social Class --> Experience of Working Together

•	We will conduct the following mediation analyses for the working together condition only:
◦	Social Class --> Average Experience of Working Together --> Task Performance

•	We will conduct the following mediation analyses for both conditions:
◦	Social Class X Task Condition --> Subjective Task Experience --> Task Performance
	
•	We will conduct all of the above analyses both with and without covariates (e.g., carefulness, familiarity) to test the robustness of our effects, and control for potential confounds.

title_r: Disentangling the assumed precursors of prejudice: Personality and social identity
abstract_r: We want to show an intraindividual variation in expressed prejudices, depending on the salience (accessibility of particular group information) of differen social identities. In social psychological research there’s a broad consensus on the fact, that individuals are either bigoted or tolerant, which seems to reflect their deep seated personality characteristics (e.g., Adorno et al., 1950). Although the original theory of an “authoritarian personality” has received much criticism and has been revised several times (Altemeyer, 1981; Feldman, 2003; Oesterreich, 1996; Stellmacher & Petzel, 2005), the basic concept of a prejudiced personality has been retained. Thus, psychological research has gathered massive evidence for the assumption that some people are more prejudiced, whereas others are less prejudiced or more tolerant (Duckitt, 2001; Hodson & Dhont, 2015; Sibley & Duckitt, 2008). The two most prominent personality variables, RWA (Altemeyer, 1981) and SDO (Sidanius & Pratto, 1999) show consistently strong positive correlations for various prejudices (Sibley & Duckitt, 2008). What’s more is the observation that these prejudices against several target groups are interrelated thus that an individual who has prejudices against one group also tend to have prejudices against other groups. This phenomenon of generalized prejudices (Allport, 1954; Ekehammar & Akrami, 2003), which is also build in Zick’s (2008) syndrome of group focused enmity, seems to be the most convincing evidence that prejudices must be part of a certain personality. However, recent research challenged the approach of a prejudiced personality (Brandt, Reyna, Chambers, Crawford, & Wetherell, 2014; Chambers, Schlenker, & Collisson, 2013; Lindner, Elad-Strenger, Hechler, & Kessler, 2019). The main criticism focuses on the Achilles heel of decades of prejudice research: its narrow focus on prejudice targets (e.g., ethnic, national, sexual orientation). Researchers may have selected the most intuitive examples of prejudice as effects to be explained (Kahneman & Miller, 1986). As Wells and Windschitl (1999) point out, the functional sample size of an experiment is very low, if the critical missing feature is stimulus sampling. As a result of the small functional sample size of prejudice research (due to the neglected stimulus sampling of prejudice targets), the understanding of the existence of a prejudiced personality has been manifested over the past five decades. In our previous study we tested the predictive validity of RWA and SDO for a broader sample of prejudice targets that included the often used conservative targets (e.g. Homosexuals) and added a set of liberal prejudice targets like Managers, Bankers and Lawyers etc. (Lindner et al., 2019). We were able to replicate the well-known observation of a strong positive correlation of RWA and SDO with conservative prejudice targets. What’s new is that we also demonstrated that individuals low in RWA and SDO are highly prejudiced towards liberal prejudice target-groups, which is inconsistent with a one-dimensional personality explanation. Moreover, both, individuals high and low in RWA and SDO have generalized prejudices toward different sets of target-groups. In addition to RWA and SDO, we measured conservatism, meritocracy and humanism as confounded ideologies. Radkiewicz (2016) has already demonstrated that the prejudice prediction of RWA is largely based on the conservatism that is built into the RWA-Scale. We replicated his finding and extended it for liberal prejudice targets. We also found that SDO shares much variance with conservatism and humanism, which, if removed, minimizes the prejudice prediction. Thus, criticism on RWA and SDO is twofold: first, the finding that individuals without the certain personality structure are highly prejudiced is inconsistent with a one-dimensional (personality) explanation. Second, the prejudice prediction of the personality variables heavily relies on its confounds with ideology. Although the previous research reveals major shortcomings of the concept of a prejudiced personality, it doesn’t offer an alternative explanation for the formation of an individual’s prejudices. Therefore, the proposed study aims to clarify the role of personality and social identity (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) within that process. Personality traits are stable over the life span and become entrenched with increasing age (Aken & Aken, 1991; Asendorpf & van Aken, 1999). If RWA and SDO are personality variables, the same should apply to them. So, if the personality of an individual predicts its prejudices and if the personality is stable over time, one should have the same prejudice pattern in different situations or contexts. In contrast, the social identity theory emphasizes the social context of individuals. An individual’s social identity is the knowledge, that (s)he is member of a particular social group and the extent to which (s)he identifies with that group. Any given individual may possess several social identities. When a particular social identity is made salient, self-categorization (Turner, 1987) is activated and individuals tend to behave more group-normative rather than idiosyncratic. So, if the identification of an individual with a particular social group lead to group-specific-normative behavior, the prejudice pattern should vary as a function of the salient group-membership.

title_r: Happy Parents Make Sad Children - A replication study
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This study examines the extent to which there is a correlation between parental relationship quality and the quality of one's own relationship experiences. Additionally, it investigates whether the similarity or dissimilarity to one's own parents influences personal relationship quality with romantic partners. Furthermore, the length and status of the current or most recent relationship will be assessed to analyze whether these factors may also have an impact on the correlation.

summary: The study aims to replicate and extend previous research on the relationship between parental relationship quality and individuals' own relationship satisfaction. It seeks to examine whether there is a positive correlation between relationship fluidity and relationship quality. Additionally, it explores the hypothesis that the correlation between parental relationship quality and own relationship satisfaction is stronger when there is a focus of similarity rather than dissimilarity. The study also predicts that longer relationships (higher relationship fluidity) will be positively correlated with own relationship satisfaction.

The study will be conducted through an online survey administered via the Qualtrics platform. Participants will be recruited from the researchers' social networks and the target population consists of university students. The survey will assess variables such as demographics, relationship fluidity, relationship status, parental relationship quality, and own relationship satisfaction.

The planned sample size is estimated to achieve a power of 90% with an alpha level of 0.05, aiming for 171 subjects based on a small to moderate effect size. The study will utilize a quasi-experimental design, employing a between-subjects approach with a manipulation of similarity/dissimilarity focus. Blinding will be achieved through the online design.

Data analysis will involve statistical tests such as Pearson correlations, ANCOVA (alternatively Johnson-Neyman test), and additional correlational analyses. Inference criteria will be set at p < .05 for statistical significance. Exclusions will be made for incomplete survey responses and individuals who have never been in a relationship.

The materials for assessment include the Children's Perceptions of Interparental Conflict (CPIC) questionnaire for parental relationship quality, specific survey questions for assessing participants' relationship quality and status, and questions on relationship fluidity (years spent in the relationship). The analysis plan emphasizes the use of appropriate statistical models to test the hypotheses.

Data exclusion will be applied to incomplete survey responses and those who indicate they have never been in a relationship. Missing data is not anticipated to be a concern.

Overall, this study's replication and extension of previous research aims to enhance the understanding of the impact of parental relationship quality on individuals' own relationship outcomes, providing valuable insights for interventions targeting family relationships.

title_r: Racial and Ethnic Variation in the Negativity Bias-Ideology Connection: A Registered Report
abstract_r: This is a Registered Report for a study of racial and ethnic variation in the relationship between negativity bias and political attitudes. Pioneering work on the psychological and biological roots of political orientation has suggested that political conservatism is driven in large part by enhanced negativity bias. This work has been criticized on several theoretical fronts, and recent replication attempts have failed. To dig deeper into the contours of when (and among whom) negativity bias predicts conservatism, we investigate a surprisingly overlooked factor in existing literature: race and ethnicity. We propose that different political issues represent threat or disgust in different ways depending on one’s race and ethnicity. We will recruit 150 individuals – 50 each of Whites, Latinxs, and Asian Americans – to examine the relationship between negativity bias and four domains of political orientation: policing/criminal justice, immigration, economic redistribution, and religious social conservatism. This Registered Report has an "in-principle acceptance" at Politics and the Life Sciences.

title_r: MB2P - Knowledge vs. Ignorance-based Violation of Expectation in Children and Adults: A combined eye tracking and pupillometry study
abstract_r: Empirical evidence in support of infants’ and toddlers’ mental state understanding comes from two experimental eye tracking paradigms: action anticipation and violation of expectation. The ManyBabies2 consortium is planning a conceptual replication of action anticipation paradigms (Schuwerk, Kampis, accepted pending data collection). A related experimental probe of young children’s ability to track others’ mental states is the violation of expectation paradigm with two dependent variables: looking time and change in pupil dilation. The key idea is that surprising events, i.e., mental-state incongruent events, result in greater looking time and pupil dilation The proposed study is a spin-off of the main MB2-study. A final scene will be added at the end of the study, i.e., after the final video was presented, in order to test the concurrent validity of using measures of pupil dilation and looking time. In this scene, the second agent (the bear) exits the tube on one of the two sides constituting goal-congruent or goal-incongruent resolutions.

title_r: How education did (and did not) accentuate partisan differences during the Ebola outbreak of 2014-15
abstract_r: Education exacerbates partisan gaps in scientific knowledge and attitudes. However, previous findings about the extent and symmetry of this moderation have been mixed. As a conceptual replication of previous research, this study examines whether education asymmetrically moderates the Democrat-Republican gap in attitudes about Ebola virus disease (EVD) and policies to combat EVD. Weighted data from a survey of 1,461 non-institutionalized adults drawn from a probability-based panel were collected during the 2015 EVD epidemic. The survey measured seven attitudes: fear of personal infection, estimated severity of Ebola, suspicion of exposed Africans, suspicion of exposed Americans, Western government preparedness, support for low-intensity interventions, and support for high-intensity interventions. Knowledge about EVD was also measured. As in prior studies, highly educated Democrats uniquely diverged from other respondents in some attitudes. However, in the other attitudes, there were main party and education effects but no evidence that education was a moderator of partisan differences. Overall, education moderated partisanship when attitudes were affect-laden and targeted toward immediate threats, but not when attitudes were policy-oriented.

title_r: Gut microbial links to human sleep
abstract_r: Sleep is crucial for human health (Luyster et al., 2012) and cognition (Diekelmann and Born, 2010). However, approx. 25% of the population fail to reach the recommended amount of sleep (Kocevska et al., 2021), which is associated with tremendous societal costs related to health care and productivity (Krause et al., 2017; Hillman et al., 2018). Sleep is controlled by the brain, acts neuroprotectively (Hobson, 2005), and is also modulated by the gut microbiome – the multitude of microorganisms that inhabit the gastrointestinal tract (Sekirov et al., 2010; Clemente et al., 2012; Cryan and Dinan, 2012). Gut bacteria produce metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids (Xie et al., 2017; Dalile et al., 2019; Colombo et al., 2021; O’Riordan et al., 2022) that engage the brain via different pathways, including the circulatory (Sudo et al., 2004) and immune systems (Singh et al., 2016), as well as the vagus nerve (Zuo et al., 2007; Bravo et al., 2011; O’Leary et al., 2018). Prior work in rodents showed that gut bacteria modulate slow-wave sleep (Brown et al., 1990) and that sleep deprivation, in turn, impacts gut microbiome composition (El Aidy et al., 2020). In humans, the gut microbiome was linked to sleep disturbances (González‐Mercado et al., 2020), self-rated sleep quality (Grosicki et al., 2020), and sleep duration (Smith et al., 2019), and this relationship appears mediated via microbially-produced short-chain fatty acids (Wang et al., 2021). A particular problem is that the majority of studies so far were based on small samples (N between 8-37 participants), assessing sleep characteristics via self-reports, thus leaving it unclear to what degree findings from animal work can be translated to humans. Here, we aim to replicate the proposed association between sleep and the gut microbiome in a large-scale participant sample and clarify its longer-term stability. Importantly, indices of self-reported sleep quality will be complemented with objective measures of sleep duration, efficiency, and composition. Gut microbial composition and function will be determined through indices of overall community structure and the abundance of specific, sleep-related bacterial taxa (Anderson et al., 2017). To quantify short-chain fatty acids, we will analyse the fecal metabolome. This multi-level approach will characterise the microbiome-sleep relationship with unprecedented detail. A clear understanding is needed as it could help to prevent insufficient sleep and ameliorate its detrimental consequences, potentially through modulating the gut microbiome. We are currently preparing a Registered Report for this project. Details of our data request to the Healthy Brain Study (https://www.healthybrainstudy.nl/en/home) are attached. The study protocol of the Healthy Brain Study can be found here: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0260952

title_r: ReFiNe-MDD: Replicability of Findings in Neuroimaging in Depression
abstract_r: The goal of this project is the systematic assessment of the extent of replicability in the field of neuroimaging, particularly of neuroimaging findings in depression research. A 'replication crisis' has emerged in an increasing number of research fields and there are indications that this could be particularly relevant in neuroimaging. However, there are almost no replications in this field yet, so the extent of the problem is unclear. Therefore, this project aims to systematically conduct a series of direct replications (copying original methods as closely as possible) of published findings of neural correlates (gray matter) of depression-associated variables. By this means, we aim to estimate the general replicability in the field and to identify concrete predictors for high/low replication probability. We will use large-scale available MRI cohort datasets with over 6000 participants from non-clinical and clinical samples. Furthermore, we aim to infer concrete implications for the improvement of neurobiological research in the field of psychiatric illness. All planned methods (including available replication samples and the planned analyses) of the overarching replication project are preregistered and can be publicly accessed (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/52B4V). Each individual replication will also be preregistered and linked to this project.

title_r: Are Men from Mars and Women from Venus? Replicating previous findings on sex differences with the Big Five Inventory-2
abstract_r: Using the Big Five Inventory-2, the aim of this study is to replicate the general pattern of results regarding sex differences in the Big Five traits Negative Emotionality (Neuroticism), Extraversion, Open-Mindedness (Openness), Agreeableness and Conscientiousness. With a few exceptions, the relevant literature generally indicates that women consistently score higher than men on all of the global Big Five dimensions. The two traits women reliably score higher on than men are Neuroticism and Agreeableness. On the facet-level, however, men consistently score higher than women on Assertiveness (E2), Energy Level (E3), Productiveness (C2) and Intellectual Curiosity (O2). title_r: Acute kidney injury in the UK: a replication cohort study of the variation across three regional populations
abstract_r: A rapid growth in the reported rates of acute kidney injury (AKI) has led to calls for greater attention and greater resources for improving care. However, the reported incidence of AKI also varies more than tenfold between previous studies. Some of this variation is likely to stem from methodological heterogeneity. This study explores the extent of cross-population variation in AKI incidence after minimising heterogeneity.Population-based cohort study analysing data from electronic health records from three regions in the UK through shared analysis code and harmonised methodology.Three populations from Scotland, Wales and England covering three time periods: Grampian 2003, 2007 and 2012; Swansea 2007; and Salford 2012.All residents in each region, aged 15 years or older.Population incidence of AKI and AKI phenotype (severity, recovery, recurrence). Determined using shared biochemistry-based AKI episode code and standardised by age and sex.Respectively, crude AKI rates (per 10 000/year) were 131, 138, 139, 151 and 124 (p=0.095), and after standardisation for age and sex: 147, 151, 146, 146 and 142 (p=0.257) for Grampian 2003, 2007 and 2012; Swansea 2007; and Salford 2012. The pattern of variation in crude rates was robust to any modifications of the AKI definition. Across all populations and time periods, AKI rates increased substantially with age from ~20 to ~550 per 10 000/year among those aged <40 and ≥70 years.When harmonised methods are used and age and sex differences are accounted for, a similar high burden of AKI is consistently observed across different populations and time periods (~150 per 10 000/year). There are particularly high rates of AKI among older people. Policy-makers should be careful not draw simplistic assumptions about variation in AKI rates based on comparisons that are not rigorous in methodological terms.

title_r: Working Together Replication Experiment
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

summary: Working Together Online Experiment Preregistration

Data Collection: We will recruit N = 800 participants from MTurk and randomly assign them to one of two task conditions: working together or working individually. In both cases, participants will complete the Lost at Sea task and will have up to 12 minutes to complete the task (Nemiroff & Pasmore, 2001).  We will limit our recruitment to only those participants who have completed at least a 4-year college degree to control for experience with problem-solving tasks and isolate the effect of social class background on task performance. We will also limit recruitment to those ≤53 years of age to increase the relevance of social class background to participants’ experiences. 

Power Analysis: We determined our sample size by conducting an a priori power analysis based on the effect size obtained in similar previous studies (f = 0.11). The power analysis indicated that we would need a final sample size of N = 708 to reliably detect our effects at 80% power. 

We anticipate that we will need to exclude roughly N = 90 participants – to account for both those who fail embedded attention check items, and those who are assigned to the working together condition but are not successfully matched with a partner (a byproduct of the Chatplat software that we will utilize to pair participants together in the working together condition; cf. Wood-Brooks & Schweitzer, 2011). We should be left with a final sample large enough to detect our effects if we recruit approximately 800 total participants.

Hypotheses: Our goal is to test the following two hypotheses:

1)	Task Performance
a.	Participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will perform worse than participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working individually condition.
b.	In contrast, groups of participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will perform better than groups of participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working together condition.

2)	Subjective Task Experience
a.	Participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will have a worse experience than participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working individually condition.
b.	In contrast, participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will have a better experience than participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working together condition.

3)	Groups of participants from working-class backgrounds (WK) will report more positive experience of working together (e.g., more integrativeness and coordination) than groups of participants from middle-class backgrounds (MD) in the working together condition.

4)	Experience of working together (e.g., e.g., more integrativeness and coordination) will mediate the relationship between social class and task performance.

Summary of Variables:
•	IV: Participants’ social class background (WK vs. MD)
◦	Measured via parental education attainment: 
WK = both parents’ highest education level < 4-year college degree vs.
MD = at least one parent’s highest education level ≥ 4-year college degree

•	IV: Task Condition (individually vs. together)
◦	Working individually: participants will complete the Lost at Sea task individually
◦	Working together: participants will complete the Lost at Sea task with a partner via a Chatplat chat, they will be put in social-class-matched pairs based on their 

•	DV: Task Performance 
◦	Yoked deviation score – will average across two similar individuals to be able to compare performance across working individually vs. together conditions

•	DV: Subjective Experience with Task
◦	Mean of 5 items: how comfortable, how natural, how well, to what extent did you perform up to your potential, how well do you think you did relative to other participants 

•	Working Together Mediator: Experience of working together (will take average of two partner scores)
◦	How much did you and your partner build on each other’s ideas?
◦	How much did you and your partner integrate each other's ideas?  
◦	How much did you and your partner seek each other’s opinions?
◦	To what extent did you and your partner share information with each other?
◦	How comfortable was it for you and your partner to work together?
◦	How natural was it for you and your partner to work together?
◦	How easy was it for you and your partner to work together?
◦	To what extent did you and your partner cooperate to get the work done?
◦	To what extent did you and your partner work together to make decisions?
◦	How positively did you and your partner respond to each other? 
◦	How much did you and your partner affirm each other's ideas? 

•	Covariate: Carefulness
◦	How careful were you when completing the task? 
◦	How seriously did you take the task?

•	Covariate: Familiarity 
◦	How familiar are you with task? 

•	Covariate: Age
◦	We wanted to focus on social class background in this study, and as such were hoping to focus on a participant population ≤40 years of age. However, according to TurkPrime, our required sample size was not feasible unless we expanded our age range to 53.

Analysis Plan
•	We will conduct a factor analysis of all the experience of working together items to determine whether they all load onto one factor. If they do, we will combine all items into a single experience of working together measure. If they do not, we will analyze them separately according to the factors that emerge. 

•	We will then conduct the following analyses of direct effects:
◦	Social Class X Task Condition  Task Performance
◦	Social Class X Task Condition  Task Performance
◦	Social Class X Task Condition  Subjective Task Experience
◦	(Working Together condition only): Social Class  Experience of Working Together

•	We will conduct the following mediation analyses for the working together condition only:
◦	Social Class  Average Experience of Working Together  Task Performance

•	We will conduct the following mediation analyses for both conditions:
◦	Social Class X Task Condition  Subjective Task Experience  Task Performance
	
•	We will conduct all of the above analyses both with and without covariates (e.g., carefulness, familiarity) to test the robustness of our effects, and control for potential confounds.

title_r: Don’t listen to yourself! A preregistered auditory distraction study about ignoring one's own voice and that of others
abstract_r: Our own voice is a very special stimulus. Of all the sounds we hear in our everyday lives, it belongs to those that we encounter most often. It is an important part of our representation in the world and a key communication tool. Other self-relevant stimuli such as our own name are known for their particularly high attention-grabbing potential, albeit it is unclear whether this is in fact due to their self-relevance or the strong call for action that is associated with hearing our own name. In this preregistered conceptual replication study, we will compare the disruptive effect of one's own voice to that of another person's voice to investigate whether a self-relevant stimulus without a strong call for action still has the capacity to capture our attention. We will use a classic serial recall paradigm with three auditory conditions: (1) A quiet control condition, (2) an own voice condition, in which participants listen to an artificially generated clone of their own voice, and (3) an other voice condition, where participants listen to the voice of their yoked-control partner. If we observe an own voice effect, we will also explore whether it habituates and is modulated by recognition or resemblance.

title_r: Second Phase: Replication and extension of Gantman et al. "The time course of moral perception: an ERP investigation of the moral pop-out effect"
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This is a second round of data collection in our replication and extension attempt due to discrepancies that were discovered part way through initial data collection.

summary: During data collection for our experiment, we observed that accuracy levels on the behavioral task were much higher than reported in the original study. We eventually discovered that this was due to a discrepancy between our method, which was consistent with the method reported in the original article, and the method actually used in the original experiment. The original experiment displayed the word and mask above the fixation cross, while we displayed the word and mask at the location of the fixation cross.

Given that obtaining useful EEG data depends on observing the expected pop-out effect and that accuracy levels at or near ceiling performance make the pop out effect much harder to detect, we decided to terminate data collection before our pre-registered target and start a new round of data collection. Our target for the new round of data collection is 65 usable samples. 

Preliminary analysis of the data that we collected in the first round has helped us to tune our preprocessing pipeline and exclusion criteria. In addition to the pre-registered analysis plan from the first round of data collection, we are pre-registering the following EEG preprocessing steps:

We will extract only the four channels of interest: Cz, Pz, Fp1, and Fp2.
We will re-reference the data to the linked ears (A1 and A2).
We will filter the data using a 0.1 to 30Hz bandpass filter.
We will segment the data to windows from 400ms before the target word appears to 1200ms after. This is a 200ms cushion around the final segment target in order to avoid edge effects in our eyeblink removal step.
After segmentation, we will remove any segments where one or more channels has an absolute voltage fluctuation of 1000 microvolts or more.
We will then baseline correct the segments using only the -200 to 0ms portion of the segment.
We will then use a regression-based eyeblink removal process. This involves averaging Fp1 and Fp2 to generate a single "eye channel", using a 200ms wide triangle filter to detect rapid rises and falls in voltage that are consistent with an eyeblink and labeling those timepoints, computing a propagation coefficient using regression between the eye channel and Cz and Pz, and subtracting the voltage in the eye channel, multiplied by the regression coefficients, from Cz and Pz, at the time points identified as containing a blink. We will not attempt to regress out EOG signals since we do not have EOG-specific electrodes.
We will resegment the data to include just the -200 to 1000ms range.
We will remove any segments that still contain absolute fluctuations of 500 microvolts or more. 
We will apply baseline correction again.
If we need to analyze data from electrode sites other than Cz and Pz after applying the data-based method for selecting the individual electrodes described in the original paper, we will apply the above preprocessing steps to the data from those electrodes.

We are pre-registering the following behavioral data preprocessing steps:

If there is clear evidence that a subject inverted the response keys (e.g., accuracy well below 50% on one or both blocks), we will apply a correction that flips the responses on the relevant block. We observed this twice in our first round of data collection.

We are pre-registering the following exclusion criteria:

If the total number of usable EEG segments in any stimulus category after preprocessing is below 75% we will exclude the subject and collect data from another participant. In our first round this occurred for one subject. All other subjects had 90% or more usable segments.

title_r: Stability and Change in the Big Five and Big Six: New Tests of the Maturity and Cumulative Continuity Principles
abstract_r: The maturity principle and cumulative continuity principle have been fundamental in understanding adult development of personality traits. We tested new predictions derived from both principles for Honesty-Propriety, a factor from the newer Big Six model, as well as for the original Big Five domains. We also tested hypotheses about lower-order Big Five aspects, gender differences in change, and a plateau in rank-order stability in early and middle adulthood. Data came from a national sample of U.S. adults (N = 858) who were assessed via both self- and informant reports in an accelerated longitudinal design with four annual waves. Consistent with the maturity principle, self-reports of Honesty-Propriety increased with age; changes in informant reports were directionally similar but nonsignificant. We also replicated previous findings supporting the maturity principle: Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Emotional Stability all increased with age. Analyses of lower-order aspects showed largely similar patterns of change at a different level of the personality taxonomy. Women increased in Emotional Stability more than men did. In tests of the cumulative continuity principle, we did not find evidence of increasing rank-order stability from age 18 to 58. This suggests a modification to the cumulative continuity principle in which rank-order stability is relatively unchanging across this period of life, what we term the working years plateau.

title_r: Sexual orientation and number of relatives in men and women
abstract_r: We aim to replicate findings resulting from the sexually antagonistic gene hypothesis (SAGH) of male homosexuality. According to this hypothesis, homosexuality in men is partly heritable and at least one genetic locus is X-linked, the relevant allele(s) residing on the X-chromosome and being transmitted to homosexual men from their mothers. This allele or these alleles should also increase fecundity of carrier women, which is in fact a mechanism considered to be responsible for pertaining of male homosexuality in human population. We will test this hypothesis as well as the so called maternal immune hypothesis (MIH), that brings prenatal mechanisms in action. The mother is presumed to be immunized by pregnancies with male fetuses, develops an immune response which raises the probability that her subsequent sons will be gay. Gay men, on average, should have more older brothers, which has actually been demonstrated by a body of research. The possibility that the relevant allele(s) reside(s) on autosomes cannot be excluded. If this is so, it could possibly be reflected in an elevated fecundity not only in female maternal relatives of homosexual men, but also in other classes of relatives. We will try to replicate previous findings of other researchers on a sample of Czech homosexual and heterosexual men and women. We will compare two methods of data collection - the questionnaires distributed either on-line or physically in field. In the questionnaire, we are going to gather information about the number of our participants' relatives and their sexual orientation. Participants will be sampled using targeted sampling method.

abstract_r:
